reading.synopsis: Psychiatrist Doctor Harris is called in to examine Corporal Westerburg, a healthy young Patrolman stationed at a remote asteroid checkpoint garrison who has calmly declared himself to be a plant and refuses to do anything but sit motionless in the sun. As the delusion spreads to twenty more of the garrison's most driven, high-achieving personnel, shock-box interrogation reveals a common thread: all were 'taught' by mysterious beings called 'the Pipers' who live in the asteroid's forest. Harris travels to the asteroid himself, and in the woods encounters and questions a beautiful, silent native girl who claims to know the Pipers and agrees to lead him to them. Returning to the Garrison, Harris confidently delivers a fully rational psychiatric explanation — the delusion is a mass unconscious projection by overworked, driven men onto the primitive, carefree natives, an unconscious wish to return to a childlike, responsibility-free existence they cannot consciously admit to wanting. That night, alone in his quarters, Harris empties a sack of soil he secretly collected onto his floor, lies down in it, and falls peacefully asleep — revealing that his own confident diagnosis was itself already the delusion's final victory over him.

structure.form: short story in three movements: the diagnosis and its spread, Harris's own journey to the asteroid and encounter with the native girl, and his triumphant explanation followed by an ironic reveal of his own affliction
movements: Doctor Harris investigates Corporal Westerburg's calm insistence that he has become a plant, and the delusion rapidly spreads to twenty of the garrison's most capable, high-achieving personnel.
Traveling to the asteroid himself, Harris meets a silent, graceful native girl in the woods who claims knowledge of the mysterious 'Pipers' and leads him deeper into the forest.

Harris returns and delivers a confident, fully rational psychoanalytic explanation for the entire phenomenon -- only to reveal, once alone, that he has secretly collected soil from the asteroid and now sleeps in it himself, exactly as afflicted as the men he diagnosed.
structure.point_of_view: third person close to Harris throughout, so the reader shares fully in his confident, ostensibly authoritative diagnostic reasoning right up until the story's final paragraph reveals that his authority was already compromised.
structure.central_device: A confidently delivered, entirely plausible psychoanalytic explanation for a mass delusion, presented with full narrative credibility right up until the story's closing image reveals the explainer himself has already succumbed to the very affliction he just explained away -- undermining the reader's trust in the rational framework retroactively rather than contradicting it directly.

characters.name: Doctor Henry Harris
characters.note: His confident, textbook psychoanalytic diagnosis -- driven, overworked men unconsciously projecting a wish to return to a carefree, responsibility-free childhood onto the asteroid's primitive natives -- is presented as entirely correct in its mechanism, which is exactly what makes his own eventual affliction so devastating: understanding the delusion perfectly did not make him immune to it.

characters.name: Corporal Westerburg
characters.note: His calm, untroubled insistence that he has simply and permanently become a plant, with no distress or urgency about it, sets the story's tone of the affliction as peaceful surrender rather than crisis.

characters.name: Commander Cox
characters.note: His blunt insistence that the affliction is mere 'goldbricking' and a discipline problem gives voice to an institutional refusal to take the phenomenon seriously until it has already spread through a tenth of his command.

characters.name: The native girl
characters.role: an asteroid native encountered at a forest pool
characters.note: Silent, graceful, and seemingly outside ordinary human urgency or time, her agreement to lead Harris 'to the Pipers' is never actually shown paying off directly -- the story leaves ambiguous whether she led him anywhere at all, or whether his own exposure to the forest and its soil was sufficient.

settings.name: Asteroid Y-3 Garrison and its surrounding forest
settings.note: A modern, highly regimented quarantine checkpoint bordering an untouched, primeval forest inhabited by primitive, carefree natives living what the story explicitly calls a 'Garden-of-Eden existence, without struggle or conflict.'

motifs: A mass psychological affliction spreading specifically among the most driven, high-achieving personnel, as though ambition itself is the vulnerability
A confidently delivered rational explanation that turns out to be simultaneously correct and useless, since understanding a temptation does not confer immunity to it
A primitive, Edenic 'natural' existence offered as an unconscious wish-fulfillment alternative to the exhausting demands of driven, achievement-oriented modern life
A story's final image silently overturning its own protagonist's closing authority, without ever directly contradicting anything he said
reading.significance: The story's structural trick is unusually elegant: Harris's psychoanalytic explanation is never shown to be wrong. Everything he says about the men's unconscious desire to shed responsibility and return to an unburdened, childlike existence is presented as genuinely correct diagnosis. The horror comes entirely from the final image, which shows that correct understanding of a temptation offers no protection against succumbing to it — perhaps because achieving full insight into one's own repressed longing is itself the final step that releases it. Harris's late-story remark to Westerburg, 'I wish I'd become a plant earlier' (spoken in-character by Westerburg but implicitly true of Harris too, given how the story ends), retroactively reframes the entire clinical interview as Harris recognizing, and being unable to resist, his own exhaustion with driven achievement.
reading.closing_note: Harris's final act -- pouring asteroid soil onto his own floor, lying down in it, and falling peacefully asleep -- closes the story in silence, with no acknowledgment or narration of his own transformation, forcing the reader alone to recognize what has happened to the diagnosing doctor himself.

distinctive_terms.label: Christianity
distinctive_terms.note: Commander Cox's joking comparison of the spreading affliction to the arrival of Christianity in high places, framing the delusion as a kind of contagious, unstoppable new religion.

thematic_links_proposed.basis: a mass psychological affliction that reveals an unconscious, unbearable longing among the most driven and achievement-oriented individuals for an unburdened, pre-civilized existence

a confidently delivered, entirely correct psychoanalytic explanation of a mass delusion that offers the diagnosing doctor no protection whatsoever against succumbing to the very affliction he has just explained

open_questions: Does the native girl actually lead Harris to the Pipers, or does the story leave this deliberately unresolved -- the text never confirms he meets them directly?
